# What It's Doing to You

> "Don't be deceived. God is not mocked, for whatever a man sows, that he will also reap."
>
> — Galatians 6:7

This is the chapter where the lies are thickest.

Most men, especially young and single ones, think they've already counted the cost of this habit and found it small. "It doesn't hurt anybody. The doctors say so." The doctors are talking about your body, and on your body I take their word. **This book isn't about your body.**

A doctor can check your blood pressure. But who checks your drive, or your nerve? Who checks whether you can hold a woman's gaze, keep a promise to yourself, or pray without flinching? No clinic runs those tests. You're the only one who can read the results, and you've been reading them for years.

So almost nothing in this chapter is a medical finding, and at the one point where the doctors come into it I'll say so. The rest is conviction, and it is the testimony of men who lived it. Check every line against your own life. If one doesn't fit, drop it. I don't think you'll drop many.

A young man rarely notices the cost, and there's a reason for it. At twenty he has energy to burn, nobody depending on him, and no partner lying beside him to notice that he's absent. He can fund the habit out of the surplus. The bill arrives later, when life starts asking for everything he has. Then he finds he's been spending a tenth of it in the dark for fifteen years.

## It isn't a landmine {-}

Some men do worry about the cost. But listen to how they picture it. They picture a landmine. It's buried somewhere in the field ahead of them, and one day they might step on it. The wife finds out. The job is lost. The body fails. Or they might walk the whole field and never touch it. Plenty of men seem to. So each morning a man checks himself over, finds that nothing has blown up, and says, "So far, so good."

Get that picture out of your head. It's the wrong picture, and it's the one that keeps you walking.

Here is a truer one. Think of a bank account that somebody dips into every day. He never takes much. It's a few coins at a time, and never enough to notice. You would spot a robbery. You don't spot this. Then years later you add it up, and a fortune is gone.

That is how this habit charges you. The cost isn't buried up ahead. **IT'S ALREADY BEING PAID.** You paid some last night, in the hour you spent and the sleep you lost after it. You paid some this morning, when you got up a little flat and a little ashamed. You'll pay some this afternoon, when your mind slides off the work in front of you. And you'll pay some tonight, when you're a little less present with the people in the room. None of it is big enough to call a disaster, and that's why you never see the total.

So don't ask whether the mine will ever go off. Ask what has been going out of the account.

## What it has been taking {-}

There is no shock treatment in this book, and there won't be any here. Nothing below will be news to you. It's a list of things you already know and have trained yourself not to look at.

### Your drive {-}

One coach masturbated daily for years, and he sums up what it does to men in three short sentences: "It kills their drive. It destroys their confidence and it numbs their hunger."

Why would it do that? His answer is the best I've heard: it hands a man the reward without the effort. Think about what a man's hunger is for. It's meant to get him up, send him out and make him build something, win someone and become someone. Then every night he tells that hunger it has already been fed. After enough years it stops asking.

That is the flat feeling. It isn't sadness, exactly. The morning after, you've got your coffee, your list and your good intentions, and there's nothing behind them. One man on the NoFap forum, ninety days out, remembered where he had been: "My drive for life was almost at zero."

A married pastor says the same from the other end. God put the drive in a husband, he says, partly so that he would pursue his wife: date her, listen to her, win her again. Take that drive somewhere else and it's spent. "I don't have it anymore", he says. The husband ends up with a book on one side of the room while his wife gets on with her evening on the other.

None of this is said to shame you. It is what the habit has been taking, a little more each year, and you are leaving it.

### Your focus {-}

C.S. Lewis put it in three words: "indulgence brings fog". Part of the fog is simple tiredness. A bigger part is that the habit takes up room in your head. A corner of your mind is always either planning the next time or regretting the last. One man who got free said it felt like "coming out from a fog". He hadn't known he was in it until it lifted. Nobody does.

### Your confidence {-}

This is the one men find hardest to believe and easiest to recognize. Why would something done alone, behind a locked door, change how you stand in a room?

Because you bring it with you. You walk in knowing what you did at midnight, and you assume it shows. The morning after, you can hardly look people in the eye.

It's worst around women. A man who spent last night using women in his head finds it hard to face the next real one this morning. He's either sizing her up or looking at his shoes. He's forgotten how to simply talk to her as a person, because he's had so much practice treating women as something else. One man who got out found that this changes too: "I feel like a better person and have a better appreciation for women".

### The way you see women {-}

Porn trains the eye. Watch enough of it and you start sorting every woman you meet, in half a second, by one measure. You do it to the cashier, to your coworker and to your friend's wife. You don't decide to. It has become how you look.

The women notice, even when you think they don't. And you lose something you may not have known you had. You lose the ability to simply like a woman, enjoy her company and want nothing from her. Lust takes half the human race and turns it into a menu.

### Your standing before God {-}

If you're a believer, you'll know this one best. If you're not, read it as "your conscience".

The Bible's first story tells it. After Adam, the first man, ate the fruit God had forbidden, he covered himself, and then he hid. God came walking in the garden in the cool of the day, and Adam was crouching among the trees. Nobody had told him to hide. Shame did it without being asked.

That's the real cost of this habit to a Christian man, and it has nothing to do with lightning bolts.

God doesn't leave. You do.

You skip the prayer because of what you did an hour ago. You sit at the back and keep quiet in the small group. You feel like a fraud with a Bible in your hand. And you start to believe you're not the sort of man who gets to answer a calling.

### Your marriage {-}

This means the marriage you have, or the one you hope to have.

C.S. Lewis saw this more clearly than anyone. Desire, he said, is meant to drive a man out of himself and toward a real woman. She has her own mind and her right to say no. The habit turns him around and sends him back into the prison of himself, with his harem of imaginary brides. The harem never has a headache, never needs listening to and never asks anything of him. And a man can come to prefer it that way.

So the husband lies a foot from his wife and a hundred miles away. She can't name what's wrong, but she can feel that some part of him is being spent elsewhere. Sometimes his body tells on him. "I knew there was a serious problem", wrote a man on a sobriety forum, "when I was losing my erection sometimes when I was with my wife". And he can't tell her, so there's now a locked room in the marriage.

If she finds out for herself, it lands as a betrayal. It doesn't feel to her like a private habit. She wonders what else she doesn't know, and whether she was ever enough. None of that is her fault.

A single man shouldn't imagine that a wedding ring will fix it. Ask any married man in the trap. He took the habit up the aisle with him.

### Your body, after all {-}

This book isn't about your body, and on your body I take the doctors' word. Here is the one place where the doctors themselves have something to add.

Men have a slang name for it: death grip. Years of the same hard, hurried habit train a body to answer to one thing only, which is its owner's hand. Then a real woman arrives, and the body doesn't know her. Some men can't finish with her. Some can't stay ready. Sex therapists and urologists see these men regularly, and they have their own drier names for it.

A medical student told his story on the NoFap forum. With his first girlfriend, "even after months, still no orgasm for me. I couldn't even get close." Then comes the sentence every man should hear: "She started to think it was her fault, but deep inside, I knew what the problem was."

Let's keep this honest. It isn't an official diagnosis, and nobody has proved the cause. One study of several hundred young men looked at those with erection trouble. They were about twice as likely to masturbate in these rough ways. That shows a link and no more. Some doctors doubt it's common. And if this is your trouble, see a doctor, because medicines and other conditions can do the same thing.

Notice what the specialists who treat this prescribe, including the ones who say the habit is harmless. They usually ask a man to stop for a while, and then to change the way he does it. This book asks you to stop for good. That is my conviction, not their prescription. If a sex therapist gives you exercises, that is treatment, so follow it and talk it through with the therapist. And the medical student? A little over a month after he stopped: "I had an orgasm during sex, for the first time in my life." For other men it has taken many months. Nobody can promise you a date. What the men who stop do report is that the body often recovers.

## Both sides of the rope are fear {-}

We tend to picture a tug-of-war. One team is fear: "It's a sin, it's draining me, I hate the secrecy." The other team we think of as pleasure: "It's my comfort and my release, the one thing that's mine."

Look at that second team again, because it's fear as well. It isn't that you enjoy the habit so much. It's that you're uneasy without it. The man who never started isn't uneasy without it, any more than you're uneasy without a drug you've never taken. The habit doesn't soothe that unease. It manufactures it.

This is also why a list of costs has never made you stop. A frightened man reaches for his comfort, and you know what you've trained yourself to reach for. So instead of stopping, men develop a set of dodges:

**"It's my life. Better to enjoy it than to live like a monk."** Fine. Enjoy it. Now tell me honestly that the life this chapter has just described is the enjoyable one. Tell me the man hiding in the bushes is having a better time than the man walking in the garden.

**"I'm single. Who exactly am I hurting?"** The man you're turning into. Your future wife will marry whatever comes out the other end of this. And apart from all that, there's you now. You're a person too.

## The shadow {-}

There's one more cost, and it's the one you'll be gladdest to lose.

Every man with this habit carries a shadow at the back of his mind. Most of the time he doesn't look at it. He jokes and works and plays with his kids. But it's there, just under the surface, and it goes wherever he goes. He knows he's doing something he despises, and he has arranged his life so as not to think about it.

It's the small jolt when the conversation turns to porn, or the half-second of dread when someone borrows his phone. It's also that vague uneasiness late at night after a bad day, which he's always blamed on the day.

The day didn't cause it. Men without the habit don't carry that shadow. King David, who wrote many of the Psalms, knew it well. In Psalm 32 he wrote: "When I kept silence, my bones wasted away through my groaning all day long."

Then he tells you what lifted it. "I acknowledged my sin to you. I didn't hide my iniquity," he wrote, and God "forgave the iniquity of my sin." The shadow goes the same way for you. You tell the truth, and you are forgiven.

Some of the gains of stopping are ones you'll notice and enjoy on purpose. You'll have the time and the energy, and you'll be done with the whole silly business of making love to nobody. But the best of them is a thing you'll notice by its absence. One ordinary afternoon you'll realize that the shadow isn't there, and hasn't been for days. You'll have nothing to hide and nothing to dread.

That day is closer than you think.
